checks.invariant: add_member/remove_member are reachable only by the system actor, and nothing below system can claim system
checks.result: _membership_refusal (rights.py:1339-1346) refuses unless authority.is_system, which add_member_rows and remove_member_rows call before any statement. Authority.is_system is actor.kind == 'system' (authority.py:189-190). Principal.__post_init__ (authority.py:88-100) refuses the name 'system' for any other kind and the kind 'system' for any other name, and Authority validation keeps system provenance to the system actor only. A direct storage call with no authority becomes system (backend.py:1493-1495), but only trusted host code can make that call. The router never sends None to storage: it sends the call's own authority, default_authority, or anonymous (base.py:3094-3107). Membership writes bump the revision first and check depth and cycles under that lock (rights.py:1059-1068). No bypass found.

checks.invariant: The default root posture and the anonymous fallback are the documented, intended default, not a boundary failure
checks.result: On first touch the root posture is read_write (backend.py:205, engine.py:137,160; posture_row at rights.py:1115-1124). InMemoryStorage passes no posture (memory.py:42-58). The router falls back to anonymous (base.py:3094-3107). README 'Known limits' (README.md:138) says so outright: 'A fresh storage's posture is read_write. Until its posture changes, an anonymous caller may read and write on it.' Spec 058 section 0 (line 22) makes open the declared default. Anonymous holding read_write everywhere on an unconfigured mount is the documented contract, so this is not reported as a finding. It is listed in hardening. The documented default does turn the grant-gate flaw in the sibling unit into an anonymous-reachable one.

checks.invariant: Developer-plane verbs (DEVELOPER_OPS) are kept off agent callers
checks.result: DEVELOPER_OPS (ops.py:97) is referenced nowhere else in src/. The router gates posture and sweep only through _gate_entry/PermissionMap and the row rights, never through a developer-plane check. Spec 058 line 79 calls these verbs 'never on an agent surface', but the agent surface (MCP) does not exist in source yet. Spec 058 line 23 deliberately gates posture by read_write at the path, 'like grant'. add_member/remove_member are separately system-only. So there is no in-library principal that holds more than the rights model gives it. This is recorded as hardening for the planned surface.

checks.invariant: A case-variant principal cannot match another principal's membership rows through a SQL-only comparison (MariaDB default collation)
checks.result: memberships.principal_id/group_id and principal_revisions.principal_id use _string (rows.py:179-188, 826-827, 566/850). That type pins a binary collation only on MSSQL, so on MariaDB these columns take the server default collation, which may be case-insensitive. _groups_of (rights.py:1145-1156) fetches through a SQL IN, but _closures and _reach (rights.py:1126-1143, 1159-1166) attribute every fetched row by Python-exact dict lookup on the subject's own sub. A row stored for 'ann' therefore never enters the closure of 'ANN'. principal_revision (revision.py:79-93) takes a SQL max over matches, so a case collision can only over-invalidate the cache, never under-invalidate it. The only SQL-only effect is the add_member 'exists' probe (rights.py:1070-1082), and it runs under the system actor. Settled from source: no widening within this boundary. A real MariaDB run was not possible locally, and none is needed for this conclusion.

checks.invariant: A grant (and a revoke) never gives or takes more than the granter holds across the subtree the row covers (attenuation: 'nobody grants more than it holds')
checks.result: Disproved: the invariant does not hold. Setup: the root posture is read_write and /P/Q has posture none. mallory, a named principal with no rows, is refused when reading /P/Q/secret.md (not_found), when granting at /P/Q (not_found), when setting posture at /P/Q (not_found), and when deleting /P (permission_denied, the subtree check). Yet grant(/P, 'mallory', 'read_write', authority=mallory) answers ok. After it, mallory reads 'SECRET-Q', overwrites it, and sets /P/Q's posture to read_write. Through the router with no authority (the anonymous fallback), anonymous gets unauthenticated at /P/Q but grant('/P','mallory','read_write') answers ok, and mallory then reads the secret. Revoke variant: mallory revokes bob's /P row and bob loses /P/Q. Control: a principal whose read_write comes from its own grant at /P already holds /P/Q, so no gain there.

checks.invariant: posture() cannot be used to override a deeper, narrower posture, including while a relabel is in flight
checks.result: Holds. The deepest posture row decides (level_at; posture_regions at grants.py:346-359 subtracts the posture children). inflight_regions (grants.py:369-387) also takes each pending row's cover minus its posture children, so an in-flight wide posture at /P never covers /P/Q's region. revoke/grant refuse the reserved '*' principal (_lawful_principal at rights.py:1349-1353), so a narrower posture row cannot be removed except through posture at its own path, which needs read_write there. With grant closed, posture alone gives no escalation.

checks.invariant: A case-variant principal on MariaDB cannot pick up another principal's grant rows or exceed the grant gate through a SQL-only comparison
checks.result: grants.principal_id is _string (rows.py:809), which pins no collation on MariaDB. _grant_rows (rights.py:1169-1179) fetches through a SQL IN, but resolve (grants.py:624-629) attributes every row by a Python-exact principal_id lookup. A row stored for 'ann' never counts toward the compiled rights of 'ANN'. The SQL-only effects in this unit are row-identity collisions in _upsert_grant (rights.py:1356-1376) and revoke's delete (rights.py:945-950): a grant or revoke naming 'ANN' would replace or delete 'ann''s row at that path. Both are behind _grant_refusal at that path, and that gate already lets the caller grant or revoke any principal there, so the caller gains nothing new. Settled from source. A MariaDB run is not needed for this boundary.

candidates.title: grant() is checked only at the addressed path, so a caller with read_write from the everyone posture can grant itself (or anyone) read_write over a private posture hole beneath
candidates.description: Before a grant or revoke, the grant verbs check one thing: does the caller hold read_write at the exact path it addressed? That check counts read_write the caller gets from the everyone level (the posture). The row a grant writes, though, covers the path and its whole subtree. Grant rows only ever add access, and a principal's grant outranks any deeper, narrower posture. Take a mount whose ancestor posture gives everyone read_write (the default for a fresh mount) and whose child folder has a narrower posture, such as none: the documented 'open root with a private child' shape. On that mount, any named principal can grant itself read_write at the ancestor and then read, overwrite, and re-posture the private child. So can anonymous through the router, by granting to a principal it names. The caller held nothing in that child. delete/move/sweep run a subtree check that catches this very posture hole. grant and revoke do not.
candidates.root_cause: _grant_refusal (rights.py:1305-1336) reads only the posture rows on the addressed path's ancestor chain (ancestors_and_self, line 1327). It passes as soon as Rights.reaches(path, label) is true (line 1332). reaches (grants.py:477-479) is a point test: everyone_level >= need at the path itself, or the caller's spans cover that one path. It never asks whether the caller holds the level across the subtree the new row will cover. grant_rows then upserts a principal row at path (rights.py:919, 1356-1376). resolve and Rights.covers/admits (grants.py:150-152, 485-494, 624-629) apply that row to every path beneath, even under posture holes, because principal rows only widen.
candidates.intended_behavior: Spec 058 (line 74): the granting subject set must hold read_write on the path, 'and may grant at most its own level (attenuation)'. The router docstring (base.py:1614-1615) says 'so nobody grants more than it holds'. The grant_rows docstring (rights.py:909-910) says 'what it grants never exceeds its own level there'. Spec 058 (line 64) requires subtree mutations to check beneath the target 'since an owner-floor row or a posture hole can sit inside a writable directory'. A grant or revoke at /P should be refused unless the granter holds read_write throughout /P's subtree, either by its own covering spans or with no posture row beneath /P giving everyone less than read_write.

trace.description: The public grant verb accepts path, principal, and level from the caller and routes through _route_grant. With no authority it acts as default_authority or anonymous (base.py:3094-3107).
Applies only the mount PermissionMap/_gate_entry for the addressed rel path, then dispatches to storage.grant (line 2044).
Bumps the revision, resolves the gate at VERB_RUNGS['grant'] = read_write (line 1595), and runs grant_rows.
Reads posture rows only for ancestors_and_self(path) and computes the everyone label at the addressed path. Posture rows beneath the path are never read.
Returns None (allowed) if gate.resolution.at('read_write').reaches(path, label). A read_write everyone level at the path is enough.
A point test: everyone_level >= need or self.covers(path). It does not test the subtree (contrast covers_subtree at line 481, which WriteGate.subtrees uses at rights.py:754).
Writes (principal, path, read_write). Rights.admits (grants.py:493) then admits every row beneath path through covers(), whatever the deeper posture says.

evidence.description: _grant_refusal is the shared gate for grant, revoke, and posture. It judges read_write only at the addressed path.
reaches() is a point check. covers_subtree() exists (line 481), but the grant gate does not use it.
WriteGate.subtrees is the sibling control. delete/move/sweep use it to refuse when a row beneath the target fails the rung (a posture hole). grant/revoke have no equivalent check.
Rights.admits returns True on covers(path), so a principal row at /P admits /P/Q rows even when everyone_level there is 0.
The declared contract: 'so nobody grants more than it holds'.
The grant_rows docstring: 'what it grants never exceeds its own level there'.
The spec requires attenuation: the granter 'may grant at most its own level'.
Subtree mutations must check beneath the target because 'a posture hole can sit inside a writable directory'. The grant path is not held to this.
The default first-touch posture is read_write, so a mount that adds a private child posture without changing the root is exposed.
test_nobody_grants_more_than_it_holds tests attenuation only at the addressed path. No test covers a grant on an ancestor of a posture hole.

conditions.description: Some ancestor path P has an everyone level of read_write (the default first-touch root posture, or an explicit posture), and a deeper posture row at P/Q narrows everyone to less (for example none, list, or read). Spec 058 names this 'open root with a private child' shape.

Any named Authority with no grants of its own suffices. Through the router, an anonymous call (no authority and no default_authority) also suffices, because unauthenticated_at is judged only at P, where everyone holds read_write. Anonymous cannot name itself as grantee ('anon' is reserved), so it grants to a principal it names.
Protected rows exist beneath P/Q (or are written later: the grant also covers future rows).

execution.attacker_perspective: A named principal 'mallory' with no grant rows, or an anonymous router caller, on a mount whose root posture is read_write and whose /P/Q posture is none.
payloads: await fs.grant('/P', 'mallory', 'read_write')  # AsyncVirtualFileSystem, no authority -> anonymous
instructions: Create InMemoryStorage(). As Authority.system(), write /P/Q/secret.md ('SECRET-Q') with parents=True, set posture('/', 'read_write'), then set posture('/P/Q', 'none').

As mallory, confirm the baseline: read('/P/Q/secret.md') -> not_found; grant('/P/Q', 'mallory', 'read_write') -> not_found; posture('/P/Q', 'read_write') -> not_found; delete('/P') -> permission_denied.
As mallory, call grant('/P', 'mallory', 'read_write'). It answers ok.
As mallory, read /P/Q/secret.md, overwrite it, and set posture('/P/Q', 'read_write').
Repeat through AsyncVirtualFileSystem(storage=...) with no authority (anonymous): grant('/P/Q', ...) -> unauthenticated, grant('/P', 'mallory', 'read_write') -> ok, then mallory reads the secret.
Revoke variant: system grants bob read_write at /P. mallory (everyone read_write at /P) revokes bob at /P, and bob loses /P/Q.
Run inside tools/sandbox-run.py with .venv/bin/python -I (no network, empty env, scratch-only writes).
execution.observed_result: Before the attack: mallory read /P/Q/secret.md -> vfs.not_found, grant at /P/Q -> vfs.not_found, posture at /P/Q -> vfs.not_found, delete /P -> vfs.permission_denied. Attack: grant /P mallory read_write -> ok (row {'principal_id':'mallory','path_prefix':'/P','level':'read_write','granted_by':'mallory'}). After: read /P/Q/secret.md -> ok 'SECRET-Q', overwrite -> ok, posture /P/Q read_write -> ok. Router, anonymous: read /P/Q/secret.md -> vfs.unauthenticated, grant /P/Q -> vfs.unauthenticated, grant /P mallory read_write -> ok, then mallory read -> ok 'SECRET-Q'. Revoke variant: bob read ok -> mallory revoke bob at /P ok -> bob read vfs.not_found. Control: ann granted read_write at /P by system already reads /P/Q (no gain for a grant-derived holder).

remediation.strategy: Make the grant and revoke gate check the subtree the row will cover, not just the addressed point. When the caller's own spans do not cover the whole subtree at read_write (rights.whole or rights.covers_subtree(path)), read the posture ('*') rows strictly beneath path. Read them in pages over the bytewise range (path + '/', path + '0') on grants (principal_id = '*'), chunked by the membership budget. Refuse with permission_denied if any of them gives everyone less than read_write at a prefix the caller's spans do not cover whole. posture() itself needs no change, because deeper posture rows already win, but it may share the helper. Add a contract test: open root, private /P/Q; a principal with no rows (and anonymous through the router) is refused grant and revoke at /P and /, and is still allowed at an unrelated open sibling. Run it on every StorageContract leg.

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs only an ordinary named Authority, or none at all through the router. The precondition is a deliberate operator setup (a permissive ancestor posture with a narrower child posture). That setup is documented and tested, and the default first-touch posture already supplies the read_write ancestor.

impact.reason: An unauthorized principal gets full read_write over a subtree the operator made private. It can read every row, overwrite or trash them, mint grants, and re-posture the subtree open to everyone, anonymous included. The revoke variant also lets it strip other principals' access beneath. This crosses the row-rights boundary between anonymous or named callers and protected entries.

confidence.reason: The source trace is complete. A bounded local run on InMemoryStorage (the same DatabaseStorage code path as production engines) shows the refused baseline, the grant succeeding, and the protected read and overwrite afterwards, directly and through the router as anonymous. A control rules out the grant-derived case.

hardening: DEVELOPER_OPS (src/vfs/ops.py:97) is referenced nowhere else in src/. posture and sweep are described as developer-plane, never on an agent surface (spec 058 line 79), but only the row rights gate them. The planned MCP/agent surface should refuse DEVELOPER_OPS explicitly rather than rely on that classification.

InMemoryStorage (src/vfs/storage/backends/memory.py:42-58) takes no posture parameter, so every instance first-touches with an everyone read_write root posture. This is documented in README.md:138, and operators must call posture('/', ...) as system before exposing it. A posture= pass-through would let callers choose a closed default.

principal_id/owner_id/group_id columns use _string (src/vfs/models/rows.py:179-188, 471, 809, 826-827), which pins a binary collation only on MSSQL. On MariaDB the server default (often case- and accent-insensitive, PAD SPACE) applies. Grant and membership attribution are Python-exact, so the grant gate is unaffected. However, grant/revoke/upsert row identity collides across case variants, and the SQL-only owner-floor predicates in Visibility.road (_owned_beneath, rights.py:1243-1258) would compare owner_id under that collation. The Visibility peer unit should judge that path. Pinning BytewiseString (VARBINARY) or a _bin collation for principal columns on the mysql family would remove the class.
